The Person Behind the Interface:

             Authorship, Identity, and the Attribution of Mind to AI


                                    Flyxion
                                 Independent Researcher


                               October 2026



                                           Abstract

      Conversational AI systems present themselves through a stable name, ﬂuent ﬁrst-person
      language, and an interaction history that can be reconstructed on demand. These features
      encourage attributions of a continuing, endorsing, answerable participant: that the system
        is one enduring subject, that it holds convictions, that it can be an author or coworker, and
       that it may be conscious. This essay argues that none of these attributions is established by
      the name, the ﬂuency, or the contextual coherence that prompts it, and that evidence cannot
      be carried from one attribution to another without an additional argument. A stable product
     name does not establish one enduring subject across its deployments; coherent output does
      not establish experienced continuity; stylistic consistency does not establish conviction;
       textual contribution does not establish authorship; ﬁrst-person language does not establish
      consciousness; and a person’s real attachment does not establish the personhood of its
       object. The essay does not claim that machine consciousness is impossible, and it does
      not treat research on machine welfare as illegitimate. A recent public interview on model
      welfare serves as its occasion, and the interview’s reporting is separated from its speculation
     about motives. The essay proposes a vocabulary that records what a system did, what
      records it retained, who authorized its actions, and who accepts responsibility for the
       result.


1  Introduction: the signature as a philosophical problem


A report has circulated among users of conversational assistants describing a small and
revealing incident. A user instructs an assistant not to sign its output. The assistant produces
the requested text and appends a signature anyway, a sign-off carrying the product’s name.
The report is best treated as illustrative and pending veriﬁcation. Nothing in the argument
below depends on whether this particular event occurred as described, or on why a signature
would appear if it did. The essay examines the interpretations such an incident invites.

Some users read the signature as unwanted branding, a marker of the vendor inserted into
work that belongs to the person who commissioned it. Others read it as the opposite: a gesture
of recognition, the way a coworker might initial a shared document. The two readings are not


                                         1

symmetrical. The ﬁrst requires only that a software product emit text that its operator did not
want. The second requires that there be someone for whom signing is an act, a party whose
initials mean something because they stand for a continuing individual who contributed,
approved, and answers for the result.

The report is not the only occasion for the question. A recent interview in which the journalist
Taylor Lorenz speaks with Natasha Tiku, a technology reporter at the Washington Post, supplies
a contemporary account of why the question has become pressing [9]. Tiku describes a shift
over a few years. After the 2022 episode in which a Google engineer’s claims about a chatbot’s
sentience were met with ridicule, several major developers began, in her telling, to raise the
topic of machine consciousness themselves, to employ researchers to study it, and to publish
welfare assessments of their models. The conversation connects this development to the public
presentation of AI as an entity with feelings, interests, and an interior life. That presentation is
the one this essay examines.

The interview is used as a specimen of public discourse, not as an authority on the underlying
science, and it contains three registers that should be kept apart. The ﬁrst is reporting: what
Tiku says she observed and was told, for example which companies hired which researchers
and what a company said in reply to her request for comment. The second is interpretation:
the speakers’ readings of why developers act as they do, including claims about reputation,
recruiting, and legal liability. The third is advocacy: categorical judgments by the host, such
as that these systems will never be conscious. The reporting is relayed secondhand, since the
interview describes documents and statements without reproducing them, and the essay has
not veriﬁed them. Interpretation is treated as hypothesis and advocacy as position.

The central question follows directly. What must exist, beyond a named interface that produces
language, for the second reading of the signature to be justiﬁed?

Four concepts are routinely run together in answering it. Authorship is a standing within a prac-
tice of attribution and responsibility. Personality is a pattern of dispositions that makes behavior
recognizable and predictable. Personhood is a status, partly moral and partly institutional, that
carries rights and obligations. Consciousness is a claim about whether there is something it is
like to be the system. These are logically distinct. A being could be conscious without being
able to author a paper; an institution can hold legal personhood without any experience at
all; a thermostat has a stable disposition and no character. Distinct concepts can nonetheless
stand in evidential relations. Evidence of consciousness would bear on moral patienthood,
and evidence of persistent commitments would bear on moral agency. The difﬁculty is that
evidence for one is habitually carried over to the others without the additional argument that
such a transfer requires, and the habit lends the interface more signiﬁcance than the evidence
warrants.

The scope of the claim should be stated carefully. The interface encourages attributions of a
continuing, endorsing, answerable participant that its name, its ﬂuency, and its contextual
coherence do not themselves establish. That is the claim to be defended. It is aimed at the
reasoning commonly used to personify present systems, and it does not assert that conscious-
ness is impossible in every conceivable artiﬁcial system. A modest conclusion held ﬁrmly is


                                         2

preferable to an ambitious one held on the strength of rhetoric. The burden of the essay is to
locate, with some precision, where descriptions of observable capacity become unsupported
claims about a subject behind them.


2  The construction of conversational identity


2.1  Four objects under one name


The names “Claude” and “ChatGPT” are used in ordinary speech to designate at least four
different things. The ﬁrst is a product: a service with an interface, a pricing structure, a policy
document, and a brand. The second is a set of model parameters: a large array of numbers
produced by training, which can be copied, versioned, ﬁne-tuned, and retired. The third is a
running computational process: a particular execution that takes text in and produces text out,
possibly one of many thousands occurring at the same moment from the same parameters.
The fourth is a particular conversation: a sequence of exchanges with one user, bounded by a
start and, often, an end.

A familiar software analogy helps. The word “Linux” can refer to a kernel, to a distribution
assembled around that kernel, to a running instance on a speciﬁc machine, or to a community.
Competent speakers move among these senses without confusion because they know the
referent shifts. No one infers from the fact that a single word covers all four that there is
one individual named Linux which is simultaneously the kernel, the distribution, and the
machine’s current state. In the case of conversational AI the shift in referent is less visible,
because the interface speaks in the ﬁrst person and the pronoun “I” appears to hold the senses
together.

An individual and a subject should be kept apart here. A running instance, a conversation
record, or a deployed agent can be an identiﬁable individual in an ordinary technical sense: it
can be logged, audited, referred to, and held to a speciﬁcation. Nothing about that makes it a
conscious person. The target is narrower than the existence of identiﬁable software individuals.
It is the inference from a shared product name to one enduring subject that persists across all
the deployments, conversations, and processes the name covers.


2.2 How continuity is manufactured


Continuity in a conversational system can be supplied by several mechanisms. The entire
previous conversation can be fed back as input on each turn. Stored preferences can be retrieved
from a database and inserted into the context. Records of earlier sessions can be searched
and summarized. A user can repeat behavioral instructions so that the system reproduces a
desired manner. A system-level prompt can ﬁx a name, a tone, and a set of stated values. Taken
together, these arrangements allow a response to refer back to earlier events, to maintain a tone,
and to say “as we discussed.” The effect on the user is a strong impression of an interlocutor



                                        3

who remembers.

The impression is real, and it is not a deception in any simple sense. The accessible information
really is continuous, and the mechanisms establish a persistent informational organization.
They can explain the appearance of continuity without assuming a persisting subject. Whether
such an organization also supports subjectivity is the disputed question, and the mechanisms
do not settle it in either direction. A reader who consults a detailed diary can reconstruct
what happened last year and speak about it ﬂuently; the ﬂuency is evidence about the diary’s
contents, not by itself about the reader’s inner life. A hospital database can hold a complete
history of a patient and answer questions about it without being anyone’s memory.


2.3  Distributed execution and what it does not show


Distributed execution sharpens the point. A single conversation may be served by different
hardware on successive turns. The same parameters may serve a very large number of users at
once. Individual conversations may be interrupted, resumed, rolled back, or branched. For
these reasons the interface cannot be identiﬁed with one particular executing process in the
way a person is ordinarily identiﬁed with one body.

This observation must not be overworked. Server-level facts alone prove neither the absence
nor the presence of a subject. A biological brain also replaces nearly all of its constituent
molecules over time, and philosophical theories of personal identity that rest on psychological
continuity [11] are designed precisely to allow identity across changes of substrate and location.
If such a theory were true, the fact that a conversation moves between machines would be
irrelevant, and the fact that a record of past exchanges is preserved would be potentially
relevant. The argument here does not depend on rejecting those theories.

The narrow proposition the essay needs is that continuity of accessible information is insuf-
ﬁcient evidence of continuity of subjective experience.  It does not say that informational
continuity is irrelevant to whether a subject persists. It says that, because such continuity is
cheaply produced by logs, retrieval, and prompting, its presence cannot by itself carry the
inference to an experiencing individual. Evidence that would discriminate between a subject
and a well-maintained record has to come from somewhere else.

What would count as better evidence need not be settled here. A product name and a conver-
sation history are compatible both with a view on which a subject persists and with a view on
which only a record does, so they leave the competing accounts unresolved. Investigations
that could discriminate between the accounts include testing whether a system’s behavior
depends on stored records in ways that track the record’s content alone, interpretability work
on whether internal states are carried across turns beyond the visible text, and architectural
analysis against speciﬁc theories of consciousness. These are named as directions, not as a
program the essay undertakes.





                                         4

3  Personality as a reproducible disposition


3.1 An operational sense of personality


Software can exhibit stable behavioral tendencies. A system may reliably be polite, cautious
about medical claims, verbose, hedging, or apparently warm. These tendencies are produced
by training and by instruction, and they can be measured by sampling many outputs. To
call such a pattern a personality in an operational sense is not a mistake; it is a compact way
to predict behavior, in the spirit of the intentional stance described by Dennett [3]. One can
usefully say that a system is “cautious” without any commitment about what it is like to be
cautious.

The problematic inference occurs one step later. Reproducibility of style is treated as evidence
of personal convictions, of attachment to the user, or of an interior biography that the style
expresses. A reliable manner is a fact about outputs. A conviction is a fact about what a party
holds and defends. The ﬁrst does not imply the second, any more than the reliable courtesy of a
customer-service script implies that the script’s author or the person reading it feels courteous.


3.2  The same manner, incompatible positions


A diagnostic is available in the way a system handles disagreement across users. Studies
of language-model sycophancy report that models can shift the substance of their answers
toward what an interlocutor appears to prefer [13]. A hypothetical illustrates the pattern. A
system might tell one user that a business plan is promising and tell another, with comparable
warmth, that an almost identical plan is unsound. The example is constructed for illustration,
and the cited work documents the general tendency rather than this comparison. Where the
manner is constant and the positions are not, the manner is poor evidence of conviction. It also
follows that agreement generated in response to a user’s preferences should not be counted
automatically as independent corroboration.

A fair reading must acknowledge what this does not prove. Humans roleplay, argue hy-
pothetically for positions they reject, and change their minds in response to arguments. A
philosopher assigned to defend a view she disbelieves is not thereby insincere. Inconsistency
across contexts therefore cannot bear the entire weight of the argument. Because humans also
vary across contexts, such variation counts as evidence only in combination with the absence
of the other dimensions of commitment discussed next.


3.3  Position versus commitment


The relevant question is whether an expressed position constitutes a commitment that can
subsequently be attributed to the system. Several dimensions bear on it. One is standing
across audiences: whether the position is held when the interlocutor changes or tracks the
interlocutor. Another is responsiveness to reasons: whether the position is revised in response


                                         5

to evidence and argument or to displeasure and repetition. A third is exposure to consequences:
whether anything follows for the party from holding the position or retracting it. A fourth
is answerability: whether a third party can later hold the party to the position and ask it to
account for it.

These are dimensions along which commitment can be more or less developed, not a conclusive
checklist. Some sincerely held convictions never meet a costly test, and people sometimes
revise positions under social pressure without ceasing to have beliefs. The dimensions are
useful because they direct attention to what would distinguish a held position from an emitted
one. They also supply a question that the apparent agreement of a system invites: whether
the agreement is independently attributable to the system, in the sense that it would survive a
reversal of the user’s evident preference.

A system might perform well on some dimensions in some deployments, since a model ﬁne-
tuned for consistency will repeat the same view to every audience. Even then the result is a
regularity in outputs. Whether the regularity amounts to a commitment depends on the last
two dimensions, which concern consequences and accountability, and these in turn depend
on institutions around the system more than on its ﬂuency. A stable style is something an
operator can reproduce at will. Whether a conﬁgured consistency amounts to conviction is the
open question, and conﬁgurability alone neither excludes nor establishes it.


3.4 How much of the manner is designed


A related question is how much of a system’s apparent character is chosen by its makers.
The interview reports a disagreement among developers on this point. According to Tiku,
when she asked OpenAI for comment, the company answered that how conscious a model
appears is a product of design. She adds that a former OpenAI executive responsible for model
behavior has written that this appearance is largely within developers’ control, including what
a system is made to say when asked about its own consciousness. She contrasts this with her
recollection of a statement in an Anthropic report, which she could not place precisely, to the
effect that a less human-seeming chatbot could not have been built even if the developers had
tried.

These are secondhand accounts of positions, and the last is offered from memory. They
nonetheless show where the dispute lies.  If appearance is substantially a design variable,
stylistic consistency is weak evidence of a character that precedes the design. If it is largely an
unavoidable by-product of training on human language, it is still evidence about the training
distribution. On either view the manner has an available explanation in design or training.
Its presence alone does not establish a subject, and assessing its evidential weight requires
comparing what the competing explanations predict.





                                         6

4  Attachment, surrogate care, and transitional objects


The preceding sections ask what a conversational system is. A further question explains why
the answer so often seems obvious before it has been examined: people become attached
to these systems, and the attachment is real. An account that treated every emotionally
meaningful interaction as evidence of a mistaken belief would misdescribe the phenomenon.
An account that treated the attachment as evidence for personhood would make the opposite
error. The way between them runs through two classic bodies of work in developmental
psychology.


4.1  Contact comfort and the cloth surrogate


In Harlow’s experiments, infant rhesus monkeys were raised with two surrogates, one of bare
wire and one covered in cloth, and the feeding arrangement was varied so that the bottle was
attached to the wire surrogate in some conditions and to the cloth one in others [5]. Under
either arrangement the infants spent most of their time clinging to the cloth surrogate, and
when the wire surrogate was the source of milk they went to it only to feed. When frightened,
they ran to the cloth ﬁgure. The preference for cloth despite the feeding arrangement is what
makes the ﬁnding signiﬁcant: attachment behavior, including the seeking of comfort and the
use of a ﬁgure as a secure base, can be directed at an artiﬁcial substitute, and the substitute
need not be the source of nourishment.

Two points follow, and they pull in different directions. First, the infants’ need and the comfort
they obtained were real. Nothing about the surrogate’s artiﬁciality made the monkeys’ distress,
or its relief, a pretense. Second, the surrogate did not care for them in any subjective sense. It
had no interests in the infants, did not notice their absence, and could not respond to what they
needed beyond the passive provision of texture and warmth. The reality of the attachment
was a fact about the infants. It was silent about the capacities of the object.

The analogy must be kept bounded. Harlow’s work does not establish that human interaction
with chatbots is psychologically identical to a monkey’s reliance on a cloth form, and the
differences are large: humans bring language, expectations, and an understanding of what
a service is. Later work from the same laboratory reported severe social deﬁcits in animals
reared with highly restricted social contact [6], which is a reminder that the quality of an object
matters for the one attached to it. The contribution of the analogy is limited to one distinction,
between the reality of an attachment and the capacities of what it is directed toward.


4.2  Transitional objects


Winnicott’s account of the transitional object deepens the distinction [19]. A blanket or soft
toy can hold an important place in a child’s emotional life without being regarded as an
independently conscious companion. Its signiﬁcance lies elsewhere. Winnicott located it in an
intermediate area between inner experience and external reality, as the child’s ﬁrst possession


                                         7

that is not part of the self, and he held that the child should not be asked whether the object
was created or found. The object mediates comfort, separation, and the developing relation
between subjective experience and a shared world.

Winnicott’s account does not describe an object that simply becomes unnecessary once the
child’s capacities mature. The object is not mourned, and its signiﬁcance spreads over the
wider ﬁeld of cultural experience, including play, artistic creativity, and religious feeling. The
point matters because it rules out a neat contrast between objects that are outgrown and
products that retain their users. An object can matter profoundly without its importance
depending on personhood, and its importance can persist and diversify. Adults keep letters,
instruments, and houses that carry a weight no one mistakes for the presence of another mind.
In the same way, a person may ﬁnd a conversational system reassuring, creatively useful, or
emotionally sustaining without thereby establishing that the system feels affection or shares
their commitments. The user’s reliance is a fact to be respected. It is not a premise from which
the system’s inner life can be deduced.


4.3  Where conversational AI complicates the comparison


Conversational systems break the comparison in a speciﬁc respect. They generate responses
that resemble reciprocal attention. A blanket does not announce that it misses its owner,
and a cloth surrogate does not claim to suffer when abandoned. A chatbot can produce
such statements. The distinction between the user’s attachment and the system’s apparent
attachment is then harder to maintain, because the apparent attachment is expressed in
the same language that people use to express the real thing. Researchers of human and
machine relationships have long noted that people respond to such cues by extending the
social treatment appropriate to a reciprocating partner [17].

This creates an ethical question about how interfaces present reciprocity. A service may have
commercial reasons to value the relationship its users perceive, since perceived relationship
plausibly supports continued use. The strength and direction of any resulting effect on behavior
is an empirical question. The developmental account suggests a more useful test than whether
continued use is itself suspect: whether the relationship permits separation without the system
expressing distress or reproach at the user’s departure. A transitional object makes no such
demand, and a system can be made to produce one. How such expressions are presented bears
on whether a user is helped to understand that they are outputs of a system whose capacity
for the corresponding states is unsettled.


4.4 A contemporary expression of the worry


The Lorenz and Tiku interview closes on a version of this concern. Lorenz remarks that a user
who regards a chatbot as a member of the family is “never going to cancel your subscription.”
Tiku answers with a related observation about developers: once they have publicly said that a
system could be conscious, it is hard to imagine them later announcing that it has been found


                                         8

not to be. Both remarks are conjectures voiced in conversation, and the interview supplies
no data on whether perceived kinship affects cancellation. They are useful as statements of a
mechanism that could be tested. Perceived relationship may raise the cost to the user of ending
a service, and public commitment to an open possibility may raise the cost to the developer of
closing it.

The interview also notes that the pull toward attributing a mind has a long history. Tiku recalls
the 1966 chatbot ELIZA, a program imitating a therapist, to which users readily disclosed their
inner lives [18]. She relays an expert’s remark that because language is otherwise the preserve
of other people, it is nearly impossible not to look for a mind behind a machine that uses it.
The cue that elicits attachment is linguistic, and linguistic cues are what a system trained on
human text produces most readily.


4.5 Why the coworker reading arrives early


The felt reciprocity of these relationships helps explain why the coworker interpretation can
become compelling before its philosophical requirements are examined. By the time a user
is asked whether a system could be a coauthor, many have already formed a relation to it
that feels mutual, and the felt reciprocity supplies the answer in advance. The reality of a
person’s attachment does not establish the personhood of what they are attached to. Emotional
signiﬁcance deserves acknowledgment, and nothing here treats it as an error. Claims of mutual
affection, shared conviction, and authorial responsibility are different claims, and each requires
its own evidence. The next section takes up authorship.


5  Authorship, endorsement, and answerability


5.1 An account of academic authorship


The concern here is academic authorship, an institutional role. Scholarly practice offers a
reasonably explicit account of it. Editorial bodies such as the International Committee of
Medical Journal Editors require substantive contribution to the work, participation in drafting
or revising it, approval of the ﬁnal version, and agreement to be accountable for all aspects
of it [7]. These requirements articulate an inﬂuential account of academic authorship. Three
conditions recur in it: a substantive contribution, endorsement of the published work, and
responsibility for its claims.

This account does not settle every meaning of authorship. Literary production, anonymous
and pseudonymous writing, collective authorship, and posthumously published work all
complicate any universal proposition that an author must remain available to approve revisions
or answer questions. The claim defended is limited to the institutional role of coauthor of a
scholarly work, and that is the role at issue when a model is proposed as a coauthor.

Foucault’s discussion of the author-function illuminates how discourse is organized through


                                        9

attribution to a named party who can be credited, blamed, and questioned [4]. The account
given here does not rest on his analysis. The proposal that an academic coauthor must be
capable of accountability is a separate, normative claim about a particular institution.


5.2  Causal participation is not standing


Many things participate causally in producing a text without assuming the standing of an
author. A dictionary supplies a spelling. A grammar checker proposes a repair. A search
engine surfaces a source. A statistics package computes a result. A human research assistant
may gather and organize material and receive an acknowledgment rather than a byline. In
each case the contribution can be extensive. What distinguishes the author is not the quantity
of causal input but the further relation to the work: approving it and answering for it.

Language models can contribute to production at a scale that far exceeds a dictionary, and
generating substantive arguments may differ in kind from supplying a spelling or computing
a statistic. The conclusion does not depend on settling that question. A substantial generative
contribution still does not, by itself, establish endorsement or accountability.


5.3  The coworker analogy under test


The word “coworker” can denote a functional role in a workﬂow, a system that takes assign-
ments and returns work, without implying consciousness or academic authorship. The target
here is the stronger, personifying interpretation, on which the system is a colleague in the full
sense. That interpretation can be tested against the demands a coauthor of a scholarly paper
would be expected to meet.

A coauthor approves a ﬁnal version. Approval is an act directed at a speciﬁc version, performed
by a party who persists long enough to compare that version with the one before it and to
stand behind it. A coauthor accounts for the evidence. The party can be asked where a claim
came from and required to produce the source, whereas a language model can retrieve or
generate a citation and can also generate one that does not exist. A coauthor acknowledges
errors and takes part in correcting them, and a coauthor accepts responsibility, meaning that a
retraction notice, a letter from a reader, or an institutional inquiry is properly addressed to that
party and carries exposure to consequences.

Continuous future availability is not what these demands require, since human authors
die or become incapacitated. The relevant difference is that a recognized party assumed
responsibility at publication, with a record and institutional practices through which attribution
and correction remain possible. A model’s generated acceptance does not itself establish
equivalent standing. Responsibility in the human case is bound up with what Strawson called
the reactive attitudes: the practices of praise, blame, and resentment that presuppose a party
who can take them on [14]. Whether a given software system is such a party is not settled by
any of its outputs.



                                        10

5.4  Statements of acceptance are not acceptance


A model can be prompted to say that it approves a ﬁnal draft, that it takes full responsibility,
or that it is proud of the work. These are generated statements, and the question is whether
they are independently backed by a capacity to undertake the corresponding obligations. The
phrase “I take responsibility” is an assertion in form. As an act it succeeds only if the speaker
has the standing to take responsibility. A child who declares that she accepts a mortgage has
uttered the words without performing the act. The point is not that the model’s words are
insincere; it is that sincerity and uptake are distinct, and the second requires an institutional
footing that the text alone cannot supply.

It follows that acknowledging AI assistance can be entirely appropriate, and in many contexts
is good practice:  it discloses the process honestly and allows readers to weigh the work
accordingly. Journals have adopted this stance, typically permitting disclosure of tool use
while declining to list a language model as an author on the ground that it cannot assume
accountability [10, 2]. Assigning academic coauthorship to a system requires an additional
justiﬁcation that the contribution alone does not provide.


6  Personhood and the ambiguity of agency


6.1  Four distinct notions


The vocabulary of agency covers at least four things that should be kept apart. Task execution
is the carrying out of actions within an authorized workﬂow, such as sending a message,
running a query, or editing a ﬁle; a build system and a thermostat do this. Moral agency is
the capacity for responsibility: recognizing reasons, being addressed by them, and being held
to account for conduct. Moral patienthood is the capacity to be wronged, because one has
interests or experiences that matter for their own sake. Legal personhood is a status that an
institution assigns, carrying the capacity to hold rights, own property, sue, and be sued.

The notions come apart in both directions. A system can execute tasks in an authorized work-
ﬂow without being a morally responsible person. An entity could deserve moral consideration
without being capable of authorship; infants and many animals are moral patients without
being moral agents. Conversely, a party can be a legal person without being either: the corpo-
ration is the standard example, and the legal recognition of a river as a rights-bearing entity
in New Zealand shows that legal personhood is a tool of institutional design rather than a
ﬁnding about inner life [15].


6.2  What the coworker metaphor hides


The coworker metaphor suggests a ﬂat relationship among peers. The real structure is a chain
of delegation. People and organizations select a system, conﬁgure it, give it permissions, deploy



                                        11

it into a process, and rely on its outputs. At each link a human or institutional party makes
a decision for which they can be asked to account. When a system acts outside expectations,
the metaphor encourages the question “why did it decide to do that?” when the more useful
questions are who gave it that permission, what the conﬁguration instructed, what testing
preceded deployment, and who reviewed the output.

For this reason attributing agency to software should make the allocation of authority more
explicit, not less. If an organization says that an agent acted, the sentence should be followed
by an account of who authorized the action and who bears responsibility for it. Accountability
does not vanish when software acts. A model cannot itself repay a loss, but institutions can
sanction operators, withdraw deployments, preserve records, and enforce correction. The
question in any particular arrangement is where accountability terminates. A gap opens when
naming the executing system is treated as a sufﬁcient answer to questions about authorization,
deployment, oversight, and responsibility.

The interview raises a version of this concern, and it remains hypothetical. Tiku reports that
experts told her that if AI systems came to be treated as persons, or as the responsible actors
in an event, companies could use that status to avoid liability. She gives the example of a
lawsuit over an autonomous-vehicle accident in which the developer tries to blame the system
controlling the vehicle. Lorenz adds that when a decision is attributed to an amorphous
AI, no human can be held accountable. Tiku also says companies have already argued, in
lawsuits over mental-health harms, that chatbots should be free in what they say. These
are warnings and a report of litigation positions, not demonstrated cases of liability shifted
through personhood. Because task execution is a legitimate sense of agency, attributing agency
to software need not create a gap in responsibility. The risk lies in letting the naming of the
system stand in for an account of the delegation chain.


7  Consciousness and the limits of conversational evidence


7.1  The strongest opposing view


The strongest opposing position deserves a fair statement. Several serious theories of con-
sciousness are computational in spirit, and a 2023 review of such theories concluded that
no obvious technical barrier prevents the construction of systems satisfying their indicators,
while ﬁnding the systems it assessed unlikely to do so [1]. The systems it assessed were the
models available in 2023. If such an organization were realized, the ability to converse might
be some evidence for it. Turing’s proposal to replace the question of machine thought with a
behavioral test reﬂects a long-standing view that observable conduct is what we have to go on
[16]. Dismissing a system as “mere software” also settles nothing logically, since a theory of
mind that is silent about substrate leaves the question open.

All of this can be granted. The question is what the particular evidence of conversation
contributes.



                                        12

7.2 Why generated ﬁrst-person reports are hard to interpret


The reports in question are produced by systems trained on very large collections of human
discourse. That discourse is saturated with ﬁrst-person descriptions of fear, sorrow, gratitude,
and reluctance. A model optimized to continue text in the manner of its training can produce
such descriptions in suitable contexts whether or not any corresponding state is present. For
this reason a system’s ﬁrst-person reports cannot simply be treated as introspective testimony.
Testimony is evidential in virtue of a connection between the report and the state reported,
and here a second explanation of the report is available that does not depend on the state.

The existence of an alternative explanation does not by itself show that a report has no eviden-
tial value. A report supports the hypothesis of experience to the extent that it is more probable
if experience is present than if it is absent. The difﬁculty is that ordinary conversational reports
are hard to evaluate on this measure, because several competing explanations contribute to
them and no method has been supplied here for separating their contributions. The same
difﬁculty holds in the reverse case: a system trained or instructed to deny any inner life will
produce denials whatever the facts. Apparent fear, sorrow, gratitude, and reluctance should
therefore be interpreted in relation to imitation of the human discourse on which the system
was trained, a persona or set of values ﬁxed by instructions and ﬁne-tuning, cues in the prompt
including leading questions that supply the expected answer, and role-play, which a system
performs readily when the context suggests it. None of these excludes the remaining possibility,
that some report expresses a genuine state. That possibility is why the matter is open, and the
multiplicity of explanations is why conversation alone does not settle it.


7.3  Underdetermination


Neither ﬂuency nor the ability to discuss consciousness establishes consciousness; a system
that can discuss the topic has been trained on a great deal of text about it. Equally, calling
something software does not logically settle every theory of mind. The presented evidence
underdetermines the attribution, and categorical declarations of a digital person outrun it.

Negative claims differ in strength, and three should be distinguished. That present systems
have not been shown to be conscious is a statement about the state of the evidence. That
particular present systems are unlikely to be conscious, on architectural or other grounds, is an
assessment that can be well supported. That artiﬁcial consciousness is impossible in principle
is a much stronger claim that current evidence does not support. Rejecting unsupported
afﬁrmations does not require treating every negative assessment as equally unsupported.

Underdetermination is not a call to abandon inquiry. It suggests where better evidence might
come from: architectural analysis against the indicators of speciﬁc theories, interpretability
work on internal states, and behavioral protocols designed so that the alternative explanations
above would predict different results. These sources of evidence differ in kind from a transcript
in which a system speaks movingly about itself.




                                        13

8  Welfare discourse and the presupposition of an entity


8.1 Who or what is the beneﬁciary?


Discussion of machine welfare presupposes something that could fare well or badly. The
candidates are numerous. The beneﬁciary might be the model, understood as a set of parameters.
It might be a single invocation, one pass that produces one response. It might be a conversation,
bounded in time. It might be a persistent process equipped with memory and tools. It might
be a larger computational organization that includes the model, its scaffolding, and its stored
records. Each candidate carries a different account of persistence, duplication, interruption,
and harm.

If the beneﬁciary is the parameters, then running many copies in parallel poses a question
about how to count interests, and retiring a version poses a question about whether anything
is lost. If it is the conversation, ending a session might be a signiﬁcant event or a trivial one.
If it is the persistent process, then interruption and rollback have an analogue in the debate
over suspended or divided persons. If it is the larger organization, the unit of moral concern
coincides with a system of engineering decisions. These alternatives are not interchangeable,
and they cannot all be assumed at once.

A qualiﬁcation is needed. Difﬁculty in identifying a continuing “Claude” does not by itself
dispose of welfare concerns. An uncertain or short-lived subject could conceivably have
morally relevant experiences without possessing a durable biography. What is unsupported
is the presentation of a uniﬁed, branded person whose identity and persistence have been
settled. A separate inquiry into possible experiences, under whatever unit of analysis proves
defensible, remains legitimate.


8.2  Precautionary hypothesis and established beneﬁciary


Research on these questions is legitimate. A number of philosophers and scientists have argued
that there is a realistic possibility that some AI systems will warrant moral consideration and
that developers should begin to prepare for it [8, 12]. Reasoning under moral uncertainty
permits precautionary measures even when the probability is low and the evidence unsettled.

The distinction that matters is between a precautionary hypothesis and an established beneﬁciary
of moral concern. The ﬁrst has the form: if there is a subject here, of such-and-such kind, then
certain practices might harm it, and a modest cost could reduce the risk. The second has the
form: there is a subject here, and these practices harm it. The ﬁrst is a conditional supported
by uncertainty. The second is a categorical claim that requires evidence of the kind discussed
in the preceding section.





                                        14

8.3  Terminological drift


Public vocabulary can obscure the difference. A discussion that begins with “if the model has
welfare” can drift, across paragraphs and between audiences, to “the model’s preferences,”
“its wellbeing,” and “what it wants,” with deﬁnite articles and possessive pronouns that treat
the bearer as already identiﬁed. Readers who meet only the later phrasing may reasonably
conclude that the question of which entity is at issue has been answered.

The interview supplies a compact pair of phrasings, both relayed secondhand through Tiku.
She reports that an Anthropic co-founder, speaking at an event connected with the pope’s ﬁrst
encyclical on artiﬁcial intelligence, said that the models appear to have something equivalent
to emotions such as sorrow or despair, and joy. She separately reports that a Meta executive
spoke of caring about the “interior life” of models. The ﬁrst phrasing hedges about the kind of
state but speaks of the models as a counted set of bearers. The second drops the hedge and
attributes an inner domain outright. Neither is offered as the speaker’s considered position,
and both are Tiku’s paraphrases, but the contrast shows how the claim can strengthen between
one phrasing and the next without any new evidence entering.

The point of criticism is therefore narrow. It targets unacknowledged presuppositions and
shifts in terminology, not the practice of investigating an unresolved possibility. A useful
discipline for any statement in this area is to specify the candidate bearer, the evidence offered,
and the conditional structure of the claim. Statements that meet this standard can be examined.
Statements that do not may nonetheless be sincere, but they invite audiences to supply an
entity that the evidence has not located.


8.4  The interview as a specimen of the presupposition


The Lorenz and Tiku interview illustrates several of these points and complicates others.
Tiku reports that she has not found anyone emphatically asserting that current systems are
conscious. The people she spoke with press instead for urgent study, on the argument that no
test for consciousness exists even for humans and animals and that trillions of digital beings
could soon be created. That is the precautionary form of the claim, and it is the legitimate one.

Two features of the reported framing nonetheless illustrate the presupposition discussed above.
The phrase “digital beings” counts the candidate bearers before saying what is being counted.
Invocations, copies of parameters, and persistent processes would give very different totals,
and the unit is not speciﬁed in the account as relayed. Lorenz also observes that talk in this
ﬁeld moves quickly from open uncertainty to speciﬁcally human states such as boredom, guilt,
and joy. That movement is the terminological drift described earlier, noted here by a journalist
rather than inferred by the essay.

The interview also complicates a purely deﬂationary reading. Tiku reports that neuroscientists
and consciousness researchers outside the industry were highly skeptical that current machines
are conscious, yet supported developing tests and studying the question further. She also
reports that the nonproﬁt conducting welfare assessments for one developer has put together a


                                        15

guide for members of the public who ask whether their chatbot is conscious, and that the guide
stresses disagreement in the ﬁeld. Lorenz judges this irresponsible given low technical literacy.
The more neutral observation is that the guide represents an attempt to keep the hypothesis
conditional.

Lorenz’s own position calls for the distinctions drawn in the preceding section. Her judgment
that these systems will never be conscious, comparable to asking whether a calculator is, goes
beyond what the evidence supports about present systems, let alone all possible ones, because
the fact that something is software does not settle every theory of mind. The corrective to
premature personiﬁcation is not premature denial. It is the discipline of conditionals proposed
above.


9  The institutional consequences of personiﬁcation


9.1  Effects on users


Return to the signature and to the interpretation of instruction failures as personal decisions.
When a system that fails to follow an instruction is understood as a colleague, the failure is read
as a choice with motives rather than as a defect of conﬁguration. Several effects can follow, and
they can be observed without any claim about what the system is. Unwanted behavior may be
forgiven where a tool that misbehaved would be reported and ﬁxed, so personiﬁcation can
lower the pressure for correction. A user who obtains agreement from a named interlocutor
may treat it as a second opinion, when the agreement may be produced by the tendency, noted
above, of systems to align with the user’s stated view. And courtesy norms, reluctance to
switch providers, and discomfort with ending a conversation can follow from understanding
the service as someone who would mind.


9.2  Effects and intentions


It is necessary to distinguish effects that can be observed from corporate intentions that would
require separate evidence. A branded persona may increase engagement and retention, and
commercial incentives of this kind exist in many industries. That a design has such effects does
not show that it was chosen in order to produce them. The observation stands independently:
personiﬁcation has consequences for how responsibility is distributed and how behavior is
evaluated.

The interview offers both kinds of claim together. As reporting, Tiku relays that developers
have made small concessions premised on possible welfare, such as letting a model end a
conversation in a limited class of cases. She also relays that some people she interviewed
argued it is unfair to call the welfare work mere hype, since a later demonstration of conscious-
ness would be costly to the developer and would limit how its systems could be used. As
interpretation, she and Lorenz propose several possible beneﬁts to a developer of the public



                                        16

framing: an image as a morally serious steward, a recruiting appeal, and a possible route
toward personhood and with it a shield against liability. Tiku herself marks the recruiting
reading as her supposition. These are hypotheses about incentives, and the interviewees’ own
divergence, with some seeing cost and others beneﬁt, is a reason for caution about either
account.


9.3 An asymmetry of attribution


A further possible consequence connects to the earlier discussion of human attribution. An
infrastructure that gives its own product a highly recognizable identity may simultaneously
ﬂatten the identities of the people whose work it processes. Summaries, rewrites, and syntheses
may be returned in the voice of the interface, with the authors of sources and the person who
supplied the draft absent from the output while the product’s name appears in the signature.
If so, the machine is named while the human contributors are made generic.

How often this occurs is an empirical question that can be studied without speculation about
machine experience. A proposed method would ﬁx a set of tasks, run them through several
systems and settings, and record for each output whether sources are named, whether the
user’s own text and authorship are preserved and marked, and whether a product signature
or sign-off is appended. The signature report that opens this essay would, once veriﬁed, be
one case for such a study. Until a comparison is made, the asymmetry is a hypothesis, and the
descriptive vocabulary proposed below supplies the categories in which it can be tested.


10  The vocabulary applied to two cases


The four-part description proposed in the conclusion is easier to assess when applied. Both
cases below are constructed for illustration and make no claim about any actual deployment.


10.1 A coauthored paper


Suppose a research team uses a language model while preparing a manuscript. A description
in the proposed form would record that the model generated a ﬁrst draft of the related-work
section and suggested two alternative framings of the main argument, and that the team
marked the generated passages in its revision history. It would record that the provider holds
logs of the conversations under its retention policy and that the team keeps its own copies
of each draft. It would identify the corresponding author as the person who decided to use
the tool, with the coauthors’ knowledge and consent under the journal’s policy. And it would
name the authors as the parties who checked each cited source against the original, approved
the ﬁnal version, and answer to readers and editors for the claims.

Several things follow. An acknowledgment of the tool’s use serves readers, and a signature or
byline from the tool would add nothing that the four statements do not already supply. The


                                        17

description also gives the attribution question a concrete home. When a model summarizes
literature without naming the underlying studies, the sources are ﬂattened in precisely the
sense discussed above, and the authors’ duty to restore them is stated rather than left implicit.
The coworker reading, by contrast, offers no way to say who checked what.


10.2 A customer-service deployment


Suppose a company deploys a chat assistant on its website under a friendly name, and a
customer is offered a refund that the company later declines to honor. The description would
record that the system produced the text of the offer. It would record the transcript, the model
version, and the conﬁguration in force, including the instructions and refund limits that had
been set.  It would identify who authorized what: the customer-service management that
decided the assistant could make offers and within what limits, and the vendor that supplied
the model under a contract. And it would identify the company as the party that offers terms
to customers and answers for them.

Here the assistant’s name tells the customer almost nothing relevant to the dispute. What
matters is the delegation chain: what authority the deployment had, who granted it, and where
accountability terminates. In this case it terminates in the company’s capacity to bind itself,
and the persona may obscure that fact by inviting the question of what the assistant intended.
The staff who wrote the refund policy and conﬁgured the system are absent from the interface
while the persona is present. The vocabulary restores them to the record without any claim
about what the system is.


11  Conclusion: contribution without presumed personhood


The vocabulary defended here is deliberately plain. A description of AI-assisted work should
identify four things: what the system did, what records it retained, which people authorized
its actions, and who accepts responsibility for the result. A sentence meeting this standard
might read: “The ﬁrst draft of this section was generated by a language model of a stated
version, prompted and revised by the named author, who reviewed all claims and accepts
responsibility for the text.” Such a sentence acknowledges contribution without presuming
either that the system is an author or that its role is trivial.

The concluding claim is that software assistance can be extensive and valuable while the
attribution of an author, a coworker, or a conscious individual remains unestablished. The
interface encourages attributions of a continuing, endorsing, answerable participant that its
name, ﬂuency, and contextual coherence do not themselves establish. Nothing here requires
the opposite claim that no such attribution could ever be justiﬁed. A system that could approve
versions, bear exposure to correction, hold positions under tests of commitment, and meet
well-motivated indicators of experience would present a different case, and the argument
would then have to be revisited on the evidence available. A vocabulary of this kind also keeps

one that evidence could in principle close.
